## What the route C experiment measured

**The problem it was testing.** The library's number types form a tower: ZZ32 inside ZZ64 inside ZZ. Each level is declared as `Integral` applied to its own name. Because ZZ32 also extends ZZ64, ZZ32 ends up being `Integral[\ZZ32\]` and `Integral[\ZZ64\]` at the same time. The compiled checker has a rule that forbids exactly that: one type may not be two different applications of one generic. About 60 of the library's 103 checker errors come from this rule.

**The two routes.** Route A keeps the rule and flattens the tower, so no type is two things at once, and teaches the interpreter coercion to make up for the lost inheritance. Route C keeps the tower and softens the rule the way the team's 2012 patents describe: a type may be several applications of one generic as long as those applications line up in a chain, which the tower's do.

**What the worker did.** It built route C completely as a shadow beside the tree and ran it on small probe programs and on the whole library. Nothing touched `main`.

**Finding 1: the softened rule alone is unsafe.** Say ZZ64 has its own `+` and ZZ32 has its own faster `+`. A call written against the ZZ64 level but handed a ZZ32 value can land on the wrong body, and compiled code then crashes with a JVM linkage error. I have been calling this the specialisation hole. To close it, C needs a second rule the patents do not contain: at every level of a chain, the declarations must agree on their return types. The worker derived that rule from Naden's write-up. With it, the hole probes are refused at compile time instead of crashing at run time. Whole C is about 190 lines in five files.

**Finding 2: the new rule refuses part of the tower.** It refuses about 25 declaration pairs, mostly ZZ64's operators seen from the ZZ32 level, and MIN and MAX on Number and QQ. Making the whole tower pass needs two more things. Seven declarations the library never wrote, such as a TIMES on ZZ32. And the checker must treat `Integral[\ZZ32\]` and plain `ZZ32` as the same type. The patents allow that only when the trait says `comprises T`, meaning "nothing is this trait except T itself". Writing that clause on the eight traits that need it makes the checker overflow its stack, with or without route C. So full C is blocked behind a checker defect nobody has examined.

**Finding 3: three problems no checker rule reaches.** A chain whose middle level adds nothing of its own dies at run time in compiled code, because the code generator writes no forwarding method for a middle level. The checker picks the top of a chain where the interpreter picks the bottom, so the two paths can answer differently on one program. And the interpreter refuses the specialised pairs outright and overflows on `comprises T` the same way. Each is separate work in the code generator or the interpreter.

**Finding 4: the cheap C gives up the middle of the tower.** C-lite allows a specialised body only at the bottom of a chain. It refuses ZZ64's operators and the MIN family on Number and QQ. In plain terms, the middle levels could not have their own fast bodies. That is the opposite of what you said matters: specialisation is a must.

**Finding 5: what switching to C later would cost.** C's checker half laid over a flattened library gives exactly the stock checker's errors, so that half can be added at any time. But I told you the reversal was one library rung in reverse, and that was too cheap. It also needs the call-site fix, the code generator's forwarding method, interpreter work, a way past the overflow, and the seven declarations. The correction is in FACTS.

In one sentence: C can be built and its checker half is cheap, but full C is blocked on a checker overflow and needs code-generator and interpreter work the record never counted, while the cheap C loses specialisation where the tower needs it most.

## What the size probes found

**The setting.** A size in a type, the 3 in `Vector[\RR64, 3\]`, is a `nat` parameter. The shadow work taught the checker to handle them. The open question was what the run time does with the 3. Compiled generic code is a template, and the loader stamps out one class per use, named with the arguments, so `Vec⟦3⟧` is a class. Design A treats a size the way the run time already treats an operator passed as a static argument: a piece of the class name and nothing more. Design B gives each size literal a tiny run-time object, so a size is a real value the run time can hold and pass, as a type argument is.

**The brief's condition.** It recommended A only if "a dispatched overload arm generic in a size" needs no more under A than reading the size out of a class name. The words: overloading is several functions under one name, chosen by argument type. When the choice cannot be made at compile time, because the argument is typed `Any`, compiled code chooses at run time by testing the value's class. That chooser is the dispatcher, and each candidate function is an arm. An arm generic in a size is one written for any size, `f[\nat s\](v: Vec[\s\])`, next to arms for fixed sizes and a catch-all. Ledger row 214 has this shape working in the interpreter.

**Probe one, that arm.** Under A the dispatcher tests whether the value belongs to a class named with the arm's own letter, `Vec⟦s⟧`. No such class ever exists, so the test always fails and the catch-all is chosen. Wrong answer, silently. The fix is 70 to 90 lines by reading, not built, with two design questions inside it. Under B the dispatcher refused to compile any sized arm at all, but 29 lines fix that and all four probe programs answer right. So the brief's condition failed, and its default A fell with it.

**Probe two, the fourth gap.** A method inside a sized object reads its own size, `len() = s`. Under A the object's class was named with the template's letter instead of the number, so the read failed. Seven lines in the loader fix it, but they change how every template's constants are handled, take a branch the team's own comment calls a problem, and have not been through the gate. Under B there is no such gap.

**Probe three, a type test on a size.** Asking at run time "is this a `Vec[\3\]`" works under both designs.

The route ask.

**What we decide.** Which route the compiled checker takes on the rule that no type may be two applications of one generic, the rule about 60 of the library's 103 errors come from. Route A keeps the rule and flattens the tower. Route C keeps the tower and softens the rule as the patents describe.

**What A does, in three pieces of work.**

- **The interpreter learns coercion.** The specification lets a wider type declare a `coerce` that converts a narrower value when nothing else fits. The compiled path has this, the interpreter does not. The rung adds it at the interpreter's dispatch, about 150 to 200 lines in six Java files. This is batch 4's first rung, it depends on nothing, and it changes nothing for programs that run today.
- **The library's tower is flattened,** as Steele flattened the compiler prelude in 2011. ZZ32 stops being a ZZ64, ZZ64 stops being a ZZ, the integers stop being QQ, QQ stops being RR64. They become siblings under Number, each carrying its own algebra, and Number loses its catch-all operators. A `coerce` on each wider type converts from the narrower one. Fourteen headers change in the library. The sites that rely on the subtyping today, 160 in the library, 207 in the tests, 37 in microGPT, keep their text and rely on coercion instead. That is read, not yet run, and it is a rung of the batch after this one, because it needs the interpreter's coercion in place first.
- **The specification is revised** where it allows a type to extend two applications, with a decision record that preserves the original text, the reasoning and route C. A rung of batch 4, flagged as an original-tree edit, the frozen copy untouched.

**What it produces.** The checker count on the flat library goes from 103 to 22, measured on a copy. The two paths agree on the tower. Every type keeps its own specialised body, since the rule stays as the type group left it.

**What it touches.** The interpreter's dispatch, the two library files, the specification's prose, and the outputs of the interpreter tests, which are re-measured. No checker change and nothing in the compiler prelude.

**What a yes commits you to.** The tower shape changes for good, reversible only at the corrected cost from the last message. The interpreter makes its coercion choice at run time where the specification's is static, on a path whose speed does not count. And one open item comes to you before it is built: the library's `SUM` runs today on Number's catch-all with an empty sum of zero, and its replacement under A is open. If any replacement would touch a line of C4, you see the diff first, as your rule says.

**What a no costs.** Full C is blocked behind the checker overflow, with no scope for that fix, and needs the code generator's forwarding method, interpreter work and seven library declarations on top. Its count is 37, not 22. C-lite avoids the overflow but loses the specialised bodies in the middle of the tower.

**Your three questions on interpreter coercion.** Can it run first: yes, it is batch 4's first rung. Does it happen in the class loader: no. On the compiled path the checker inserts the conversion at compile time, so the bytecode carries a plain call. On the interpreter it is a choice made at dispatch in the evaluator. Will the JIT remove the overhead: on the compiled path there is only a plain conversion call, which the JIT inlines like any other, and the interpreter's cost does not count by your own rule. Your question (1), ℤ inside ℚ by coercion: under A, yes.

1:# Multiple instantiation exclusion: the ground for the decision
3:Gathered 2026-09-22 for Pavol's decision after rung P of climb batch 3 stopped: does the compiled path keep the designers' rule that no type may extend two instantiations of one generic? Nothing here decides. Sources are the rung's stop report and judge's ruling on `origin/wip/rung-exclusion-relax` (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-relax/REPORT.md`, `JUDGE.md`), the papers, the checker, the interpreter, the specification, and seven interpreter probes in `mie-probes/` (each `X.fss` with its capture `X.walk.txt`).
5:Terms. **Multiple instantiation inheritance**: a type extends two instantiations of one generic, for example `object Both extends { Tag[\String\], Tag[\ZZ32\] }`. **Multiple instantiation exclusion**: the rule that forbids this. **A specialised generic overload**: a generic declaration with a non-generic one beside it for one instantiation, `pick[\X\](t: Tag[\X\])` beside `pick(t: Tag[\ZZ32\])`. **Return type rule**: when a more specific overload can be chosen at run time, its return type must fit the less specific one's.
9:- The OOPSLA 2011 paper, `Papers/Types/exclusion.tick:141-152`: "Fortress imposes a rule that forbids *multiple instantiation inheritance*, in which a type (other than Bottom) is a subtype of distinct applications of a type constructor. ... We call this rule *multiple instantiation exclusion* and adopt it here." A footnote limits it to invariant parameters (`:145-150`). The stated cost is `:154-156`: "easy to enforce statically, and experience suggests that it is not onerous in practice: it is already required in Java".
11:- What it costs: "we cannot define hasStringAndInt <: { Has[String], Has[ZZ] }" (`:470-472`). The trade-off is "specialization of generic functions or multiple instantiation inheritance, but not both" (`:477-478`). The outcome: "Ultimately, Fortress implements blanket multiple instantiation exclusion for the semantic benefits and the simplicity of the restriction" (`:496-497`).
14:  - Per-trait syntax: "allow some generic traits to be multiple instantiation excluded and others not" (`:475-477`).
20:- `checkP` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:443-456`): two trait types exclude when any pair of their ancestors has the same constructor with type arguments that are not equivalent (`pEqv`, `:450`). It is one of four clauses joined at `:457`. It cannot simply be deleted: with `negate` set, the same clause gives the equality constraints that static-argument inference uses (`explorations/perf-probes/prelude/exclusion-trace.md:214-217`).
26:- Its exclusion (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/types/FType.java:197-297`) has no instantiation clause. The last test compares the leaves of `comprises` clauses (`:281-297`).
27:- Its overload check marks a generic parameter pair that neither subtype relation orders (`interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:451-455`). It refuses that pair unless some parameter pair excludes (`:495-500`, "non-ground types need exclusion"), with the message "with generic type, at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types" (`:527`).
39:- Exclusion is the smallest relation: "the relations are the smallest ones that satisfy all the properties given in those sections (and this one)" (`Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:187-189`). None of the listed properties makes two instantiations exclude (`:163-164`, `:212-216`, `:222-224`). So the type is allowed.
46:- `checkP` causes 61 errors at 23 declarations on 26 lines (`exclusion-trace.md:24-28`, `:208`; `exclusion-trace/sites.tsv`, counted by declaration):
53:- The comment "Hack to permit any Number to work non-parametrically" (`.fsi:1814`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3023`) sits on `SumReduction`. `SumReduction` is a `CommutativeMonoidReduction[\Number\]` whose `join(a: Number, b: Number): Number = a+b` (`.fss:3033`) works only because `Number` carries the algebra at `Number`. It also lists `DistributesOver` at two instantiations in the api and four in the component (`.fss:3026-3029`, where `MaxReduction[\Number\]` appears twice). `DistributesOver[\E\]` has no methods; it is "marking for distributivity" (`.fsi:1768`). So the library uses multiple instantiation deliberately in two ways: the tower's self-typed traits, and marker facts.
65:- What this means for the tower: no peer combines nested numeric subtyping with self-typed traits; every one has a flat tower plus conversions. The peers that allow multiple instantiation choose the instantiation statically, which is the specification's call-site model. Naden's hole appears only with dispatch at run time over reified generics, which is Fortress's combination.
70:- On that lineage, exclusion of two instances of one invariant constructor (the pair itself only, "If a trait A[T] does not have variance annotations then A[B] excludes A[C] unless B=C") entered on 2010-05-28 (`5a6b7913b`, jrhil47). It was extended to all ancestors as `checkP` on 2010-07-26 (`e828b44b1`, jrhil47, "Made exclusion and subtyping work together as described in the paper").
77:- The compiler prelude went flat in 2009: its four widths began as sibling objects under `Number` on 2009-03-03 (`b2880c05c`, chf), `ZZ32 extends ZZ64` and `RR32 extends RR64` came on 2009-03-30 (`76c267f98`, jmaessen), the subtyping was cut on 2009-08-31 (`6896886fb`, dr2chase, "ZZ32 is NOT a subtype of ZZ64, RR32 is NOT a subtype of RR64"), and the first exclusion, `ZZ32 excludes ZZ64`, came on 2009-10-16 (`3e0306166`, sukyoungryu). Guy Steele commented out the comparison `extends` when adding them on 2011-07-15 (`b3c2e1342`), and added the operators of the sibling `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` on 2011-07-22 (`da5291587`).

Yes, in practice. Nothing in A locks the checker, and nothing in C needs the tower to have been flat or nested from the start.

- **A touches only the library and the interpreter.** Its two rungs are the interpreter coercion mechanism and the 14 rewritten headers. C's checker half (the forest test in `checkP`, `comprises T` on seven traits, the return-type rule) is independent of that and can be added at any later time.
- **Going A then C costs one library rung in reverse.** Re-nesting means restoring the 14 `extends` links from the record (the keep note's sketch lists them), about the same size as A's library rung, and deciding what `Number`'s catch-alls become. Under remedy (i) no test or program text was changed, so there is nothing to undo there; the flat sketch is fully documented.
- **The coercion rung is not wasted either way.** The spec has coercion regardless of the tower's shape, the compiler prelude uses it, and the interpreter lacking it is a gap under every route. Under a re-nested tower the width coercions simply stop firing.
- **What is lost on a reversal:** A's library rung, about half of A's cost (1.6 M by batch 3's rate), plus the recorded spec deviation and its tests, plus any output changes accepted in between. The other order, C then A, throws away C's derived rule and checker work instead, which is the larger and less certain piece.
- **C can stay alive cheaply without being the route.** Its checker half exists as a measured shadow; the missing piece, the return-type rule, can be probed on a branch with the nested tower whenever you want it tested, without touching `main`.

The one genuine one-way element is the switch-over itself: once the compiler checks the one library in A's shape, code written for the compiled path afterwards assumes it. A return to C then also re-checks that code. A probe of C's rule before the switch-over would tell you whether that door is worth keeping open.

Recorded in POSITIONS as reactions, not decisions (`b49f6a4ef`). Answers per question:

**1, coercion.** Today a `ZZ32` value *is* an `RR64`, so `Number`'s catch-all `+` takes both. Under coercion they are separate types, and the library declares a conversion, `RR64 coerce(z: ZZ32)`, which the compiler inserts wherever an `RR64` is expected and no declaration applies without it. That is the spec's own mechanism between `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`, and the compiler prelude already runs on 15 such lines. What you keep: `x: RR64 = someInteger` works, mixed arithmetic works, row 330's decision stands with "promotion" restated as "coercion". What you give up: ℤ as a subtype of ℚ in the type relation itself, and `Empty extends List[\T\]`. The one known open item: generic code over mixed widths, where the join of a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` becomes a trait without arithmetic; the brief lists it as unsettled.

**2, the forest rule and POPL 2019.** A correction: the published path did not continue the forest route. POPL 2019 keeps the rule for invariant traits, allows two instantiations only when a single minimal ancestor exists (a cousin of the forest rule, for covariant traits), keeps specialisation by checking the return type at run time (the option Naden rejected), and has no self types and no numeric tower. So on the tower, the group's last published word is "rule kept, no nesting", which is A's shape. The forest rule survives only in the patents, filed on the last day and never built. Your "yes" stands as your weighting; the fact underneath it is narrower than you read it.

**3, which files survive.** Recorded. Route A stays on the table.

**4, the specialisation shortcut.** Two things get called specialisation. One: the class loader stamps out a class per type argument, like C++ templates. Every route keeps that, and unboxing will build on it. Two: a hand-written special version of a generic function for one instantiation under the same name, `dot(v: Vector[\RR64\])` beside `dot[\T\](v: Vector[\T\])`, picked at run time by the value's type. That is the shortcut; the exclusion rule exists to make it sound; B forbids it. Your "as long as it runs fast" is an answer: keep it unless someone shows fast without it, and nobody has. So B is out on your own terms, which the brief also concluded.

**5, run-time coercion in the interpreter.** The spec says the checker decides at compile time where a coercion goes; the compiled path does that already. The interpreter has no checker, so it can only find out at run time, at dispatch: when no overload matches, try the declared coercions. Same program, same answer in the normal case, the choice made later; that is the divergence. Not the class loader (that is the compiled path's). JIT: not relevant here, the interpreter is our oracle, not the target, and its speed is irrelevant by your rule. On the compiled path a coercion is a static call to a small function, inlined by the JIT, costing the boxing every operation pays today until unboxing lands. Can it run first: yes, that is A's first rung, 150 to 200 lines in six interpreter files, no library line changed, the gate green throughout because today's tower needs no coercion.

## Decisions on record

### The standard and the sources

- P-25 **The specification stays the standard, the Types chapter beside it.** Where the Types chapter of the team's unfinished 2012 restart (F-166) covers a topic, it is cited beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word. On the rules that the revival revises, it is their latest intent, which the goal is to finish. It covers the exclusion rule, as instantiation exclusion in its two-part form, the `covariant` modifier, and `Bottom`, which no program can write.
- P-26 **The type group's late positions outweigh the specification's early text where they conflict.** The early text was a wish. The type group then made the language run, for performance and with specialization a must, and learned what is feasible. So their later word wins: the exclusion rule, specialization kept, the compiler prelude's tower flattened in 2009 and 2010 (P-43), Naden's 2012 write-up, the POPL 2019 paper. The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text. The revival does not second-guess them: it knows less than they did.
- P-27 **The library's own practice is the standard.** What microGPT invented goes into the standard library, in the library's own style. Whoever extends the library first studies how it does the same kind of thing, and follows that pattern; exclusion, for one, is all over it. He had to find the diagonal's override himself (P-88) because that study was skipped. No fix is designed from the specification alone or from a workaround on the user's side.
- P-28 **Fleshing out the standard library is a very important task.** Next is the algebraic layer: `Ring`, `Field` and what the matrices and tensors of machine learning need, so that the library's traits reach them. It goes into the standard library itself (P-27), not into a tree of the revival's own.
- P-29 **Walk's speed is irrelevant to every judgement of Fortress's performance.** Walk is hundreds of times slower than Python's interpreter. So no performance decision of any kind, and no edit of C4, the flat model program, for speed, until microGPT runs compiled. The gate never runs the two microGPT programs, too long-running to be tests: it compiles them and records the phase that each reaches. A run of them, once possible, goes to a stage that does not gate.
- P-30 **The microGPT walk check after a batch runs in under a minute.** It runs about two forward-and-backward passes against the reference values, which shows that the model's mathematics still works and that the library's changes did not break it. The full check programs run only when asked. A slower check is to him a waste of time.
- P-32 **The territory map (`coordinator/map/`) maps the tree down to where the design intent is written, in the papers as well as the specification.** It exists so that nothing on record is found again from scratch.
- P-95 **Every change to the specification is recorded with its reason.** No discrepancy between the specification and the implementation stays open to confuse a reader. The original text and the reasons are kept, so that route C, the way back to the patents' forest rule (P-43), stays open. Every change takes the S1 form (P-96). `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is never touched.

Almost. Batch 6's rung F flattened seven types in one go: `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ` and `RR64`, each a sibling under `Number`. `RR32` was the one exception, and the exception came from the batch record, not from the rung.

**Why it was left:**
- Your coercion table didn't mention `RR32`. The draft record said any coercion beyond the table was a stop, so a worker who made `RR32` a sibling would have hit a forced stop at the first float.
- The review of that record kept `RR32` below `RR64`, the interpreter's existing shape, because the flat-tower sketch had kept it there on the grounds that it adds no instantiation.

**Why it's wrong, found by batch 6's conformance review (finding 3):**
- The specification says no number type is a subtype of another (`numbers.tex:536`), and the later Types chapter says the same.
- The compiler prelude has `RR32` as a sibling that `RR64` coerces from, the shape Chase gave it when he cut the subtyping in 2009: "RR32 is NOT a subtype of RR64".
- The mixed case is gated as an expected failure since rung F: `RR32` plus an `RR64` (row 435).

So rung V finishes the flattening. It's in 6.5 because that batch collects the repairs the conformance reviews called for.
